issues.legal_issue: A sovereign ruler could create a binding special estate through a Farman, with the property held by successive heirs apparent for a designated purpose.
material_facts: The ruler issued a Farman directing that a historic complex be kept separate from his other property and that its ownership and possession pass to each succeeding heir apparent.
The Farman directed that the complex's historical character and its association with the dynasty be maintained.
issues.conclusion: The Farman had the force of law and validly created a special estate distinct from both the ruler's personal property and State property, to be held by each succeeding heir apparent.
issues.legal_principle: The command of a ruler of an Indian State had the force and potency of law, and the ruler's sovereign will could create a special estate without conforming to established forms or patterns. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision in reaching this conclusion.

predicates.property_title_dispute: A civil dispute concerns who holds title to property.
predicates.sovereign_ruler_issued_farman: A ruler exercising sovereign authority issued a formal command concerning the property.
predicates.farman_separated_property_from_other_ass: The command treated the property as separate from the ruler's other assets.
predicates.farman_assigned_property_to_successive_h: The command directed that successive heirs apparent hold the property's ownership and possession.

issues.definition: When a title dispute concerns property separated from other assets and assigned by a sovereign ruler's command to successive heirs, the designated successors hold it as a special estate.

issues.legal_issue: A building that forms part of an integrated special estate cannot be treated as separately owned by the State merely because the ruler did not list the estate among his personal properties at merger.
material_facts: The disputed building was found to be part of the integrated historic complex governed by the Farman.
The Farman treated the complex as neither the ruler's personal property nor State property and assigned it to successive heirs apparent.
The ruler did not list the complex among his personal properties when the States merged.
The claimant was a succeeding heir apparent, while the State claimed ownership of the complex.
issues.conclusion: The building remained part of the integrated complex, the omission from the personal-property list did not defeat the claimant's title, and the State had no title to the building.
issues.legal_principle: The Farman created a special estate that was neither personal property nor State property. Because the complex was an integrated whole, its component property could not be divided between owners; omission from a list of personal properties did not defeat title to property that was not personal property. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and building_is_part_of_integrated_complex and complex_was_assigned_to_successive_heirs and ruler_omitted_complex_from_personal_property_list and state_claims_ownership

predicates.property_title_dispute: A civil dispute concerns title to property claimed by a State and a successor to an earlier titleholder.
predicates.building_is_part_of_integrated_complex: The disputed building forms part of a larger property treated as one integrated complex.
predicates.complex_was_assigned_to_successive_heirs: An earlier sovereign command assigned the complex to successive heirs apparent.
predicates.ruler_omitted_complex_from_personal_prop: The ruler did not include the complex in a declaration of his personal properties at the time of a political merger.
predicates.state_claims_ownership: The State asserts that it owns the disputed property.

issues.definition: If a State claims a building within an integrated complex assigned to successive heirs, omission of the complex from the ruler's personal-property list does not give the State title to it.

issues.legal_issue: Payment of a licence fee is not necessary for a licence to exist, and long duration alone does not defeat the characterization of possession as permissive.
material_facts: The claimant characterized the State's occupation as permissive and in the nature of a licence.
No licence fee had been paid or agreed to be paid.
The State had occupied the building for a long period.
issues.conclusion: The claimant's characterization of the State as a licensee could not be rejected merely because no licence fee was paid, and the length of the occupation did not alter that conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882, payment of a fee is not an essential attribute of a licence; the judgment also refers to Sections 60, 61 and 62 concerning licences. The length of permissive occupation does not, by itself, change its character. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: license_occupancy_dispute and occupant_possession_was_permissive and no_license_fee_was_paid_or_agreed and occupation_was_longstanding

predicates.license_occupancy_dispute: A property dispute concerns whether an occupant's possession is under a licence.
predicates.occupant_possession_was_permissive: The claimant allowed the occupant to possess the property permissively.
predicates.no_license_fee_was_paid_or_agreed: The occupant paid no fee and the parties had not agreed that a fee would be paid.
predicates.occupation_was_longstanding: The occupant remained in possession for a long period.

issues.definition: When possession is permissive, neither the absence of a fee nor the long duration of occupation negates its character as a licence.

issues.legal_issue: Longstanding permissive possession does not, by itself, become hostile possession sufficient to establish adverse title, particularly where the property has a unique impersonal character.
material_facts: The State's possession began permissively, and it continued for a long period.
The property was part of a special estate with a unique and impersonal character.
No issue of adverse possession had been claimed in the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The State's long permissive possession did not establish adverse title to the property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a claim based on adverse possession requires possession that is adverse, not merely permissive. Permissive possession does not become hostile by the mere passage of time; the Court also relied on the property's unique and impersonal character and the absence of an adverse-possession issue in the courts below. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: title_dispute and adverse_possession_claim and possession_began_permissively and possession_was_longstanding and property_has_unique_impersonal_character

predicates.title_dispute: A civil dispute concerns title to property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: An occupant relies on possession as a basis for claiming title against another titleholder.
predicates.possession_began_permissively: The occupant began possessing the property with permission rather than hostile to the titleholder.
predicates.possession_was_longstanding: The occupant remained in possession for a long period.
predicates.property_has_unique_impersonal_character: The property has a distinctive character as an impersonal estate rather than ordinary personal property.

issues.definition: Longstanding possession that began permissively does not establish adverse title where the property has a unique impersonal character.

issues.legal_issue: A mandatory injunction requiring the State to vacate property to which it has no title must be obeyed within a reasonable time.
material_facts: The State occupied the disputed building and claimed title to it.
The lower appellate court issued a mandatory injunction requiring the State to hand over possession, and the High Court upheld that order.
The Supreme Court found that the State had no title and that the injunction's terms could otherwise be evaded or delayed.
issues.conclusion: The State was required to carry out the mandatory injunction within a reasonable time; the Court directed compliance in full no later than three years.
issues.legal_principle: Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, concerns mandatory injunctions. The Court affirmed the injunction and clarified the time for compliance to ensure that the relief was effective. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: mandatory_injunction_suit and state_occupies_property and state_has_no_title and court_has_ordered_state_to_vacate

predicates.mandatory_injunction_suit: A civil proceeding seeks a mandatory order requiring an occupant to vacate property.
predicates.state_occupies_property: The State occupies the property in dispute.
predicates.state_has_no_title: The State does not hold title to the property.
predicates.court_has_ordered_state_to_vacate: A court has ordered the State to hand over possession by vacating the property.

issues.definition: When the State occupies property without title and a court orders it to vacate, the State must comply within a reasonable time.
